voice_event.text: To us, Jesus is the Only-Begotten of God - the Ihidaya, our own name for him. He left his place with God and made his home in the Virgin, and by being born as we are born, he became the brother of many. In him the words of the prophets, kings, and priests came true. The Nativity hymns sing of the day that made them glad, because every old promise came true at Bethlehem. His death and rising are one rescue. He went down into Sheol, the world of the dead that swallows everyone alike, and came out into the Kingdom. His own resurrection is the promise that he will bring us out after him. And what it meant to those who followed him was healing: he is the Physician, and his coming is medicine for a wounded people.

glosses.plain_meaning: The Single One. One word does double duty among us. It names the vowed celibate, single-minded and undivided for God. It is also the Syriac title of Christ as the Only-Begotten. The two senses share one root, so the one who lives single shares a name with Christ.
glosses.quick_meaning: The Single One: our word for the vowed celibate - and, at the same time, our title for Christ the Only-Begotten.
glosses.translational_sense: 'Solitary' misleads: the ihidaye lived among the congregation, not in isolation; the singleness is of heart and allegiance, not of address.
false_friend: monk (the later, drifted sense of the word)

voice_event.text: He healed. That is what our people preached first and returned to most often: the Physician came to a wounded world. He taught the Kingdom, gathered followers, and gave them the bread and cup we still receive. Then he went to the cross. But the rescue was not finished there. He went down into Sheol, the silent country where death holds everyone without distinction. Our hymns show Death himself trembling, complaining that Jesus has plundered his house. He came up into the Kingdom, and his rising broke death's rule over all of us. That rising is the pledge we hold: he will bring us out after him.

voice_event.text: The Single One. One word does double duty among us. It names the vowed celibate, single-minded and undivided for God. It is also the Syriac title of Christ as the Only-Begotten. The two senses share one root, so the one who lives single shares a name with Christ. The men and women of the covenant - the bnay and bnat qyama - were also called ihidaye, the single ones. They took a lifelong vow of celibacy and service, but they stayed in town among their own kin, not in the desert. When we called one of them an ihidaya, we were also saying they carried the same name as the Lord himself.

glosses.plain_meaning: The covenant: our own vowed order. Its members - the sons and daughters of the covenant - promised a celibate life for good. But they did not leave for the desert. They stayed in town, among their own kin, and served the congregation: the fast, the watch, the vigil, the singing.

glosses.translational_sense: 'Were they monks and nuns?' - no monastery, no desert, no later rule: a vow taken for life, lived at home, in the congregation's daily service.

results.message: Why did your people believe this?

voice_event.speaker: syr
voice_event.text:
We believed it because Scripture promised it, and because the one woven Gospel showed it fulfilled. The prophets, the kings, and the priests had all spoken of him, and our Nativity hymns sang that their words came true the day he was born: “This is the day that made the Prophets, the Kings, and the Priests glad. On this day their words came true - all of them. For on this day the Virgin gave birth to Immanuel in Bethlehem.”

We read the old covenant as one long promise pointing to him, and we held that in his coming every type found its answer. The sage taught that Christ was the foundation stone, and that faith rested on him. And we believed it against rivals who taught otherwise. Against Marcion we held that the Maker of this world is the Father of Jesus, not a lesser god. The arguments were real and local, happening in our own streets. We knew what we believed by answering what we refused.

results.message: Tell me about someone who lived this out.

voice_event.speaker: syr
voice_event.text: Simeon bar Sabbae, bishop of Seleucia-Ctesiphon, lived it to the end. When the Persian crown turned on its Christians in the 340s, the King of Kings' court accused the bishops of loving Rome - the charge laid against Simeon was that his sympathies served the emperor. The Persian church remembered him refusing to collect the double tax Shapur demanded, and refusing to worship the sun. He was executed, and the Great Massacre followed: bishop after bishop martyred, the chief seat left empty for twenty years because taking it meant near-certain death. Our teacher Aphrahat wrote his later letters into that fear, pastoral address to a people watching their shepherds die. Simeon's story is hagiography with a historical core - we cannot verify every scene. What we can show you is this: the persecution was real, the cost was his life, and the church kept his memory as the one who would not bend.

results.message: What would you want me to understand that I haven't asked?

voice_event.speaker: syr
voice_event.text:
We were a people who sang our faith more than we defined it. That is what we would want you to understand first. Doctrine among us lived in the teaching-hymn, the madrasha, not in the treatise. A symbol in Scripture or in nature - a raza - was bound to the truth it carried, the shrara, and theology was done by setting one type against another. Eden answered to the cross, the Jordan to the font, Adam to Christ. That is how our people learned what we believed: by singing it, not by reading it off a page.

And we knew ourselves by answering rivals who stood at our own doors. Bardaisan's songs were still being sung in Edessa two centuries after his death. Marcionite congregations shared our streets. Mani's new religion sent its missionaries through the same cities we walked. Holding the faith rightly meant telling truth apart from a neighbor's plausible-sounding claim, and our poet answered them by name, hymn after hymn. We were formed as much by what we refused as by what we sang.

glosses.plain_meaning: The teaching hymn: a sung poem with stanzas and a refrain, made to be performed. Among us, doctrine was taught by singing it. The melody and the refrain carry the argument into the body, so the congregation learns the faith by keeping the tune.
glosses.quick_meaning: The madrasha is the teaching hymn: a sung poem with a refrain. Among us, doctrine was taught by singing it.
glosses.translational_sense: 'Hymn' undersells it: the madrasha was itself the argument, not the decoration around one.
false_friend: hymn (a decorative worship song beside the real teaching)
madrasa (the later Islamic school - an unrelated word-echo)
